title: "Expect fake messages": A load of Steam user personal info has been stolen thanks to a cyberattack on one of Valve's partners, claims report
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Seemingly, only Europeans are affected

If you live in Europe and have bought hardware from Steam in the past three months, then watch out, your personal information might have been stolen thanks to a cyberattack on one of Valve's shipping partners.

"Between July 29 2026 and August 1, 2026, a cyberattack hit CEVA Logistics, the company that ships Steam hardware to customers in Europe," reads a Valve email published by Gaming On Linux's Liam Squires-Hand, which has also been shared separately by Reddit users. "CEVA is still investigating this attack, but as Valve learned on August 7, certain information about Steam customers, including you, was likely compromised." CEVA have apparently "isolated the affected systems, taken all offline and brought in outside investigators".

According to the email, CEVA obtains delivery info from Valve, including your name, phone number, email, and postal address, when shipping Steam hardware to people in Europe. CEVA retain that info for up to 90 days after order. If you've been mailed about this by Valve, it doesn't mean your data has definitely been pinched: the email notes that Valve have decided to contact anybody "we can assume were impacted".

Seemingly, you don't need to worry about credit card information or nuking your Steam logins, as "CEVA does not have access to your payment information, passwords, Steam Guard codes or other information".

If you have fallen victim to the CEVA hack, you can look forward to a bunch of spam. "Expect fake messages - email, SMS or phone - that mention your hardware order and appear to come from Steam, Valve or a delivery company," the email reads. "They may quote your address back to you to prove they're genuine. They may ask you to confirm a delivery, pay a small customs or redelivery fee, or sign in somewhere to 'verify' your order. Treat all of them as fake."

The email notes that Steam Support never handle issues over email, Steam chat or Discord, so don't believe anybody who tries to hustle you on there. Also, don't click any links you get in suspect emails – type in the Steam store address yourself. And don't give anybody your password or Steam Guard code. All pretty standard safety malarkey.

The email promises that Valve are "pressing CEVA for the full scope of what was taken and how, and we are in the process of notifying the data protection authorities in the countries affected, including yours."

It seems unlikely, but not impossible that the email itself is a really tortured bluff on the part of some wily cyberburglars, designed to trick you into lowering your guard somehow. One can never be too careful, and I have duly sent Valve a request for clarification via channels I trust. I wrote all of it in capital letters to make sure they take me seriously. Whatever the truth of the matter, none of this is going to help sell Steam Machines.

title: Where to find the Shimanoyama region Treasure Hunt in Forza Horizon 6
author: Sean Martin
content:
The new summer Horizon Mascot Party Festival Series has arrived in Forza Horizon 6, and that means a new weekly Shimanoyama Treasure Hunt, plus more challenges and rewards. There are also two seasonal cars you can progress towards, the Exomotive Exocet Sport and the Datsun 2000 Roadster, and completing this challenge will give you a little bit of progress towards earning them. All that said, here's where to find the chest.

Forza Horizon 6 Shimanoyama region Treasure Hunt location

This week, the treasure chest is located at the Shimanoyama Drift Circuit in the far north-east of the Shimanoyama region. All you need to do to find it is:

  1. Head towards the circuit
  2. Turn off to your left and head under the sign towards the entrance
  3. Turn left into the circuit itself
  4. You'll spot a bunch of open garages on your left side with advertising banners on top—the chest is in the third garage along

Simply smash into it as usual and you'll get 100,000 credits, 5,000 XP, and 3 Season Progress points towards those two Summer Season cars.

For more progress, make sure to complete the photo challenge at Hokuryu Sunflower Farm, plus the weekly challenge involving the Toyota Japantakushi.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Sean's first PC games were Full Throttle and Total Annihilation and his taste has stayed much the same since. When not scouring games for secrets or bashing his head against puzzles, you'll find him revisiting old Total War campaigns, agonizing over his Destiny 2 fit, or still trying to finish the Horus Heresy. Sean has also written for EDGE, Eurogamer, PCGamesN, Wireframe, EGMNOW, and Inverse.

title: Invisum Piscium 嫌魚 is a dreamlike walking sim about fragments of conversations and a deep craving for water fish haven't procreated in
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
You know, the regular stuff

I won't dive into why this is happening to me at the moment, you'll either need to pay me £20 or let me pay you to be my therapist to get that explanation, but I've been having some odd dreams lately. They're frequently temporally confused, mixing and matching people from across my life that should never have crossed paths. This has left me looking to ground myself a touch, so of course I decided to take a look at Invisum Piscium 嫌魚, a walking sim that's not quite about dreaming, but is about looking for distilled water that's free from fish sex contamination.

Invisum Piscium 嫌魚 is upfront about what it is on its Steam page. Atmosphere and exploration come first, there are "almost no traditional puzzle elements," you can pick up items and use them to "subtly alter the world." There's no question about this in the demo either. It opens in a bathroom, a rubber duck in front of you on the side of the bath. Of course you interact with the rubber duck, and it speaks back to you.

You leave the bathroom and find the main room in the apartment, a woman that looks like a plush doll brought to life starts talking to you about how she's losing her mind over the fact that fish mate in water, so she's feeling anxious about drinking it and asks for some distilled water. The quest begins! What follows in the demo, the process of getting to its ending (which does not see you acquire the distilled water) reminds me of the trading sequence in Link's Awakening, albeit in a smaller scale.

A depressed goth with a cat plush gives you a cake. She feels empty. You give the cake to a bunny girl, and she explodes and dies, so you bring her back to life with an energy drink. You find some money, so you buy a snack, and give it to the goth, and the exchange of miscellaneous goods continues. Ghosts float around the apartment complex you find yourself in with the goth and bunny girl, spouting cryptic messages. In the distance you can see the clouds, the corners of the skybox as clear as day and you wonder what the limits of this world are.

The demo for Invisum Piscium 嫌魚 isn't all that long, and it's not clear how big the full game would be. It certainly feels like it sits in conversation with indie classic Yume Nikki, and more recent games like nophenia. How far we'll all be lulled into its dreamlike world is a question that's yet to be answered. You can check out Invisum Piscium 嫌魚 for yourself on Steam.

title: Until Dawn and Little Nightmares 3 studio Supermassive announces further layoffs, with as many as 75 people expected to lose their jobs
author: Matt Wales
content:
"This is a necessary step to ensure the sustainability of our company."

Supermassive - the UK studio best known for its cinematic horror games including Until Dawn, The Quarry, and the Dark Pictures Anthology series - has announced more layoffs, this time affecting as many as 75 employees.

"We have made the difficult decision to begin a redundancy consultation process, which we anticipate will result in the loss of up to 75 of our colleagues," the studio wrote in a statement shared on social media. "This is a necessary step to ensure the sustainability of our company.

"We know this will be an incredibly difficult time for everyone," it added. "And our priority throughout the process will be to provide support to all those impacted."

Today's planned redundancies mark Supermassive's third round of job cuts in the last two years. In July 2025, it announced layoffs affecting up to 36 employees, saying the move was necessary to "adapt our team structure to better align with recent industry changes".

That followed confirmation of a "reorganisation" in February 2024, which the company said would impact "some" of its team. While the studio's statement didn't expand on that number, a report by Bloomberg claimed 150 employees had been told their jobs were at risk, and that 90 redundancies were expected.

Supermassive most recently released its cinematic sci-fi horror adventure Directive 8020, the fifth entry in its Dark Pictures Anthology series, which launched to mixed reviews in May. That was preceded by Little Nightmares 3 last October, which saw Supermassive take over the much-loved horror series from original studio Tarsier with equally mixed results.

title: Halo Studios seemingly cut staff after Halo: Campaign Evolved launch, including a 6-year veteran producer
author: Mark Warren
content:
"It has finally caught up to me"

Update: Game Developer cite a source familiar as having told them that Halo Studios staff have "departed as a result of external contractor shifts" and that no full-time staff have been laid off.

Original story below:

Halo studios appear to have cut an unspecified number of staff following the release of Halo: Campaign Evolved last week. A number of contract workers at the studio have posted about their departures on LinkedIn within the past day or so. Halo Studios' parent company Microsoft, lest we forget, laid off around 1600 workers in early July, while parting ways with several of the studios that had been under their umbrella.

"After 6.5 years working on Halo and dodging just as many rounds of layoffs - it has finally caught up to me," Halo Studios producer Nick Treitman wrote in a recent post. "I have nothing but love for Halo and the folks at the studio, this is just a tough reality in the gaming industry right now."

Meanwhile, Paul Morris - a scrum master on Campaign Evolved with previous producing credits The Last of Us Part 2 Remastered and Forza Motorsport 7, shared a similar story. "Today, I learned my time at Halo Studios will be coming to an end following the successful launch of our latest game, Halo: Campaign Evolved," he wrote. "I know this is one of the most challenging job markets our industry has seen, and I know the road ahead won’t be easy. But I’m not done, and my purpose has not changed."

Both Treitman and Morris' LinkedIn profiles indicate their roles at Halo Studios to be contract ones, meaning it's possible the company have opted not to renew such deals following Campaign Evolved's launch, rather than having laid off full-time staff as Microsoft did last month. Not that that would be any less terrible - the result in both cases is people out of work at a time when, as the pair acknowledged, losing your livelihood is especially tough to bounce back from.

I've contacted Xbox for comment.

Microsoft's recent cuts have affected a vast swath of the big name studios the company own, including Bethesda, Obsidian, Id Software, and ZeniMax.

title: As fans hunger for an update on The Division 3, Ubisoft quietly releases mobile free-to-play game The Division Resurgence to miffed reviews on Steam
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Give me another Clancy.

The Division Resurgence is a name you may have forgotten. In the sea of announced-then-cancelled off-shoots based on Ubisoft's biggest franchises, Resurgence was one of the few to actually make it to release.

The free-to-play loot shooter has been available on iOS and Android since March, and later made its way to PC in April - though only on Ubisoft's Connect launcher in early access. Resurgence then arrived on Steam last week, though despite Ubisoft announcing the Steam release in June you may not have noticed given how little fanfare surrounded it.

Player reactions on Steam are about as negative as you'd expect, with many questioning why Ubisoft released a game clearly designed for mobile devices on PC in the first place. At the time of writing, it's sitting at a 'Mixed' rating with nearly 1,600 user reviews.

"Honestly… just get the regular game you need to pay for. This one is just way too wonky as a mobile port of the regular first Division game and the play style just overall sucks to deal with," one review reads.

Others shared criticisms about the game's free-to-play aspects, which they say contribute to a worse experience.

"All the loot is locked behind daily completions, and you only get to do those maybe four-five times a day. Then the game scales the xp and rewards down hard," another review reads.

Despite the volume of user reviews, player turnout hasn't been all that. The game peaked at just 4,117 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB) at launch, and its 24-hour peak is even lower.

The reactions are understandable when you consider that Ubisoft continues to support The Division 2, the mainline sequel that's been running since 2019. The game even broke its all-time concurrent record on Steam earlier this year. Indeed, the original Division also remains playable on PC.

Resurgence was initially announced back in 2022, when it was expected to arrive in 2024. That obviously never came to be. Seeing as it's mostly based on the first game's New York map, you may be better off playing The Division 1.

Meanwhile, part of the reason this release has rubbed players the wrong way so noticeably is likely Ubisoft's lack of updates on The Division 3. Despite having been announced in 2023, the developer-publisher has been largely silent on the project. Notably, creative director and longtime franchise lead Julian Gerighty departed earlier this year, though Ubisoft released a statement at the time assuring fans development remains on track.

"Our teams who built this world with Julian are still here, carrying it forward with an ambitious, unchanged commitment for the future of The Division 2, The Division 2: Survivors, The Division Resurgence, and The Division 3," the company said.

title: "There's a huge amount to be learned" - how the pioneering years of gaming are being preserved for a new generation in a corner of south London
author: Matt Wales
content:
Wander the winding track to London's Kingston University over the next week and you'll find a little pocket of gaming history awaiting there. The Archive of Retro Computing (ARC) is free to explore and features over 65 retro personal computers and gaming consoles, some familiar and others considerably less so. It's an exhibit stretching from the mid-70s and the advent of video game cartridges to significantly more modern gaming consoles, charting the history of personal computing across an incredibly rich three decades.

Paul Neve, the man behind ARC, is the course leader for undergraduate computer science at London's Kingston University. And when I videochat with him ahead of this year's showcase, he's against a corkboard backdrop festooned with nostalgic magazine ads. "The heart of a system that grows with you!", exclaims one spread for the ZX81; "Why do girls like Atari Computer Camps?", ponders another.

We are, it turns out, of a roughly similar age; children of what Neve calls the "glory days" of computing. His own journey begins with the Atari 2600, and he would later graduate to the 8-bit era of personal computers - the Sinclair Spectrums and Commodore 64s - charting a path through the likes of ZX81, the Spectrum 128, the Spectrum +2, the Atari ST, and eventually toward more recent consoles like the PlayStation 1 and original Xbox. "I suppose growing up in that era," he tells me, "it's why I do what I do".

As we reminisce, he pinpoints the Spectrum as his "first true love", and he vividly recalls having "a face like a smacked backside" after taking his Christmas and birthday savings to WH Smiths in his youth, only to discover he was £17.29 short of the £49.99 asking price - at which point his dad took pity on him. As for his favourite game, that'll be designer Matthew Smith's legendary platformer Manic Miner, even all these years on ("Maybe I'm just a dinosaur, but I find it very difficult to put in the investment of time for modern titles", he says). Yet despite Neve's obvious passion for the computer industry's pioneering years, it turns out the Archive of Retro Computing is a relatively new collection.

"A couple of years ago," he tells me, "one of my colleagues had a contract with a house clearance company ... and this eccentric engineer had basically been buying everything from 1970 onwards. So it really was like the motherload. The house clearance company wanted to auction it all off. But the chap there said to my colleague, 'Is there anyone who knows about this stuff? We really think it should be exhibited before it actually gets sold off.'" And this, of course, is where Neve joins the story.

That initial collection was exhibited in 2004, and the showcase proved enormously successful. "After that one, I got the bug as it were and then I proceeded to effectively emulate the eccentric engineer by then pretty much buying everything," Neve says. "If you like, it's my midlife crisis, because any computer or console that my childhood self [would have liked], I basically went and acquired."

Today, Neve's collection totals somewhere between 70 and 80 machines, ranging from the early generation of 3D consoles - the PS1, PS2, first Xbox, and Dreamcast (all newly added) - to home computer classics like the Commodore and Spectrum, and a number of "unicorns". There's the Fairchild Channel F, for instance, one of the first home consoles to use a microprocessor and one of the first to use removable cartridges, known as Videocarts. Then there's Smith Engineering's vector-based Vectrex, first released in 1982. "That's an absolute classic", he enthuses. "I love that one so much I went and bought one for home." He's even managed to acquire a Sam Coupé ("effectively the Son of Spectrum", as Neve puts it); a short-lived machine developed in Swansea by Miles Gordon Technology that was also one of my own brief obsessions until I learned what a SNES was.

The success of now-ARC's first showing in 2004 "opened the door at the university", Neve explains, and the institution is being "incredibly supportive" now, providing a space not just to store his collection but to exhibit it too: "They get the benefit of it bringing people into the university and so we use it at open days as well." Kingston University's Town House is hosting ARC's third annual showcase event this week, and for Neve, the first hope is that visitors - it's open to the general public - have fun. But more than that, he'd also love them to walk away with some knowledge they didn't have before. "We can learn so much from these machines of the past," he says, "and that informed the very first exhibition we ever ran.

"When I organise the exhibition, there is a narrative," he explains. "There's obviously the consoles. But in terms of the computers, you've got 'The Battle of Britain' that tells the Sinclair and Acorn story. You've got 'Thank you for your service'. That's the American story; the Commodore, the Apple, the Texas Instruments, the Atari story. And then there's 'They could have been a contender', and I think these are my favourite ones ... brilliant machines where some small company, some engineer, had a vision and a dream and released something that was technically superior to your Spectrums etc. and then they just got squashed by the big boys. There's the Memotech MTX, a gorgeous-looking big old long, sleek black thing ... There was a whole raft of also-rans, your Dragon 32s, but below those were these fireflies, released on the market for about six months then the company went bust."

But ARC isn't just about preserving the history of the machines themselves; it tells the stories of the individuals behind them too. "Clive Sinclair. Chris Curry [who] worked with Clive Sinclair," Neve continues. "He was at Sinclair Research until they had a falling out and Chris Curry went off to found Acorn. And that entire personal rivalry, what we know about that one-upmanship between those two, it pretty much motivated the entire British computer industry in the 80s." And there's the story of Jerry Lawson, the co-designer of the game cartridge thanks to his work on the Fairchild Channel F, and also one of Silicon Valley's first Black computer engineers.

"Preserving stories like that, the stories of the individuals, we can learn [so much] as computing professionals, games developers, even designers in general - some of our user experience design lecturers quite enjoy the physical design of the machines and bring their students in to explore their iterations from generation to generation. The Sinclair machines are great at that: the ZX's rubber keys to the Spectrum Plus; the designer of those, Rick Dickinson, is brilliant."

Neve has found the collection useful in his own teaching too. "Increasingly I've come to realise that ... in terms of the pedagogy of programming, we've fallen into a very scripted way of working," he explains. "In my day, [there was] what pedagogic theory calls bricolage, the idea where you just tinker and experiment.

"A few years ago, a student said to me, 'I don't think this assessment was fair ... we had to write a tic-tac-toe game in Java [and] you never told us how to write a tic-tac-toe game in Java.' But that's why it's called an assessment. Increasingly, there's this expectation there's going to be step-by-step instructions - step one, type 'public class tic-tac-toe', step two, type 'static void main string args', Step 474, close curly brackets - then, 'Congratulations, you have just written a game!' No, you haven't. The bloke who wrote the tutorial wrote it. You just were his pen.

"And so what the retro machines do for that sort of thing is they get [students] back to basics; literally back to BASIC. It presents them with, effectively, a flashing cursor and invites them to experiment without the distractions of Instagram and YouTube and all the things we use computers as: media consumption devices, entertainment devices ... This just puts them in programming and they've got nothing else to do. And as they tinker and they start seeing things happen, it encourages them to want to do more ... They experiment and learn by doing, rather than getting the impression they're learning by following step-by-step instructions."

All this talk of retro computer programming suddenly takes me back to the hours - days - of my youth spent diligently copying code from Your Sinclair and Input magazine in the hope of getting a rudimentary game running at the end of it all. And it's a thought Neve picks up, drawing comparisons with the online tutorials of today.

"YouTube videos effectively have [viewers] typing out the code and that's not the same as what we used to do. We used to type in listings from magazines [and] you make mistakes. You have to debug it. You have to try and figure it out. You'll mistype something and if it runs and does something weird, you're going, 'Why is that doing that weird thing?' And you're looking at what you've typed and you're looking at what you should have typed ... and that teaches you."

It might be a bit of a tangent, but for Neve, it's all part of the magic of a collection like ARC: "There's a huge amount to be learned, and not just for us tech heads. Lessons to be learned from a business perspective, interesting stories, fun to be had. All of which disappears without things like ARC to preserve them."

It is, of course, a pertinent time to be discussing preservation: grassroots consumer campaigns like Stop Killing Games are fighting to save online games from disappearing; Sony (spurred on by a discless GTA 6) has announced plans to ditch physical media, and soaring hardware component prices threaten to hasten us toward a cloud-based gaming future. So I wonder, if games become ephemeral and consoles and computers are intangible, how much more can ARC grow? What kind of history can the modern medium hope to accumulate?

"Potentially very little", Neve replies, "because it can be reinvented at the drop of a hat. You'll have enthusiasts, hackers ... I'm sure people will find a way, but once we go into full-blown streaming and all you're getting is an image, there's nothing to capture ... They'll still release games [but] the history becomes discontinuous.

"I was reading an article the other day about how if there was an asteroid that suddenly wiped out human civilisation, a subsequent successor civilisation is going to go, 'What happened after the 80s? We've got no idea' - because we stop writing things down, we stop putting things on physical media; the same is going to happen with games."

But future aside, Neve's current work continues, and there are big things planned for the Archive of Retro Computing, which is set to become a permanent exhibit at Kingston University from September. The current intention, Neve explains, is to run regular events for students and more intimate events for the public throughout the year between ARC's big annual showcases, including gaming events focusing on the individual franchises, retro coding events, and more.

But even with a permanent home, not everything can be displayed at the same time. "We've got what we're going to call residents," Neve continues. "They're your Mega Drives, PlayStations, even the older ones like the Ataris that everyone coming to a retro show is going to want to see. But then on the edges, we've got room to rotate things so we can get the rarities, the obscure ones out.

"If we're doing retro coding events, we can populate the fringes with Spectrums and BBCs: things that are good to do retro coding on; the more obscure games consoles that we wouldn't regularly exhibit, we can get those out. There's a whole gamut of computing history, gaming history, console history. So many stories to tell within that. So, we're looking forward to it. I think it'll be a lot of fun." And it might, suggests Neve, even encourage guests to become "miniature preservationists" too.

It's an optimistic thought as we face an increasingly transient gaming future, but perhaps that's the real power of collections like ARC: not only that they help us remember, but that they remind us why it's important to remember too.

This year's ARC Annual Showcase Event runs from 5th August until Tuesday 11th August at London's Kingston University Town House, KT1 2EE. Doors open at 10am to 6pm on weekdays, and 11am to 4pm on the weekend. Entry is free and booking isn't required.

title: Two Beloved Characters Are Coming to Disney Dreamlight Valley In Free Updates
author: Ashely Claudino
content:
Follow

Link copied to clipboard

Published Aug 15, 2026, 11:01 AM EDT

Two new characters will join Disney Dreamlight Valley this year! Fans are in for a treat — and a few tricks

Disney Dreamlight Valley will receive two major free updates later this year

Sign in to your Polygon.com account

Disney Dreamlight Valley's roadmap for the rest of 2026 has been announced, revealing a massive expansion pack and two free updates. It seems that every month of the year will bring new characters to the Valley, giving players a lot to look forward to before the new year rolls around.

A previous content roadmap for Disney Dreamlight Valley revealed that players would learn more about two upcoming free updates in August. More information was revealed during D23, an event with panels and announcements related to Disney's many franchises, like one confirming the mutant cast of the upcoming X-Men movie.

During a Disney Dreamlight Valley panel, this year's content roadmap was fully uncovered. It was revealed that fans will soon be able to dress up as Hannah Montana and Lizzie McGuire, as outfits from the shows hit the Premium Shop starting Aug. 19.

Besides that, Oogie Boogie from The Nightmare Before Christmas and Lilo from Lilo and Stitch will be making their way to the Valley in September and December, respectively. Oogie Boogie joins the player once they complete the yearly Halloween event. With Lilo's arrival, Stitch will no longer have to wander the Valley by himself; the two will be reunited at the end of the year for a holiday-themed update. As per usual, fans will most likely have to complete themed quests and help these characters settle in before they're ready to move into the Valley.

Lastly, but certainly not least, the theme of the previously teased paid DLC was confirmed. Players can take their Disney Dreamlight Valley adventure to the deep sea with The Keepsake Sea, featuring none other than Captain Jack Sparrow. An exact release date has not been revealed, but it will drop in October, between the free updates.

As a 'thank you' for tuning in, players can claim the free D23 Varsity Jacket 2026 as an exclusive cosmetic. All they need to do is open the Help section in the Settings menu and input the code: "DDVD23PANELGIFT". It will be placed in their in-game mailbox. Fans can watch the entire panel on the official Disney Dreamlight Valley YouTube channel.

title: "Litigation Often Takes a Toll on a Party's Mental Health on Both Sides of the 'v'"
content:
From Doe v. Simons, decided July 29 by Judge Nicholas Ranjan (W.D. Pa.):

Plaintiff John Doe has moved to proceed under a pseudonym. Doe advances three main bases for anonymity: his mental illness; that requiring him to litigate under his own name would deter him, and similarly situated individuals, from pursuing litigation; and that his HIPAA-protected medical records would become public….

Doe has not shown that he faces a reasonable fear of severe harm. Doe's case appears to be a straightforward employment-discrimination case. And where plaintiffs allege a fear of severe harm (namely heightened mental illness symptoms and stigma) in ordinary employment-discrimination cases, like this case, courts have denied motions to proceed under a pseudonym. See Doe v. Coll. of New Jersey (3d Cir. 2021) (affirming district court's denial of plaintiff's motion to proceed pseudonymously where the district court … "observed that, with regard to a need for anonymity, [plaintiff's] case was not meaningfully different from other employment disputes"). This Court has seen many cases like this one, and recognizes that litigation often takes a toll on a party's mental health on both sides of the "v."

But the mental-health effects of litigation are, in a sense, the cost of doing business. Doe has not shown the Court that the mental-health effects of this particular lawsuit are so exceptional compared to other similar cases where plaintiffs have proceeded under their legal names. See Kimberly Davis v. Surefire Hospitality Group (W.D. Pa. 2026) ("[T]he distress [here] is more properly characterized as embarrassment or discomfort, which the Third Circuit has found to be insufficient to meet the standard. Without particularized allegations, Plaintiff's request reflects a personal preference, rather than a reasonable fear or severe harm.")….

[O]ne of [Doe's] main concerns is that his sensitive, HIPAA-protected medical information will be publicly disclosed. But the Court has already granted several of Doe's motions to file documents under seal. And many similarly situated individuals have filed lawsuits within this district. The Court stresses one of the most important [factors related to pseudonymity litigation]—that there is a universal public interest in the identities of litigants—and notes that this factor significantly outweighs Doe's alleged fear of severe harm….

title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges and admits shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO
content:
News

Mandatory Credit: Photo by SARAH YENESEL/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock (16049970a) New York, New York, USA, 08 December 2025.

Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges and admits shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO

Luigi Mangione on Friday has pleaded guilty to the two remaining charges against him in the death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in December 2024. The charges of interstate stalking resulting in death and stalking through use of interstate facilities resulting in death, filed in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, both have a maximum penalty of life in prison without parole.

“I shot Mr. Thompson and he died. I knew what I was doing was illegal,” Mangione told the court during his allocution. He also said that he had never been treated or hospitalized for any mental illness or addiction, and that his mind was clear during the hearing.

Mangione does not have a plea deal with the federal government. Instead, he will face sentencing on December 18. Federal prosecutor Jamie McDonald said that the government would seek life imprisonment.

On January 30, Judge Margaret Garnett threw out two of the four charges against Mangione, including “murder through use of a firearm during and in relation to the stalking crimes charged…” A conviction on this charge would have made Mangione eligible for the death penalty.

Mangione still faces state charges in the case, scheduled for September 8. Mangione’s defense lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, filed a motion to dismiss the state’s second-degree murder and firearms charges, arguing a violation of due process and double jeopardy.

New York’s double jeopardy (when previous prosecution bars subsequent prosecution) statute is broader than the protection offered by the US Constitution. However, it includes nine narrow exceptions. Friedman Agnifilo’s motion argues that none of the exceptions apply, but she preemptively challenged CPL § 40.20(2)(b), “Each of the offenses as defined contains an element which is not an element of the other, and the statutory provisions defining such offenses are designed to prevent very different kinds of harm…” and 40.20(2)(f), “One of the offenses consists of a violation of a…provision of another jurisdiction, which offense has been prosecuted…and …been terminated by a court order…founded upon insufficiency of evidence to establish some element of such offense which is not an element of the other offense.”

In court for his guilty plea, Mangione for the first time described how he learned where UnitedHealthcare would hold its annual investor convergence in December 2024.
